brief.head: Gates, philosopher
brief.text: Ajay Shah cited “the great philoso­pher Bill Gates”: the world changes less than you think in one year and more than you think in ten. {081-C02}

brief.head: Danger near home
brief.text: Ajay Shah likened Ding’s late slip to the hik­ing les­son: the worst ac­ci­dents hap­pen when you think you have al­most reached home and let your guard down. {081-C03}

brief.head: Know your origin
brief.text: Every path leaves its own strengths and blind spots, Ajay Shah said. Know them with­out whin­ing or beat­ing your­self up, then com­pen­sate for weak­nesses or bet big on strengths. {081-C08}

brief.head: It takes a village
brief.text: Movements need more than di­rect doers like Anand and WestBridge, Ajay Shah said. They also need com­mu­nity or­gan­is­ers who keep morale and en­thu­si­asm going. {081-C16}

brief.head: Lost without a guide
brief.text: Ajay Shah wor­ried that Chess960 loses the fa­mil­iar board ca­sual fans know. Amit Varma replied that with­out great com­men­tary, fans would be just as lost in clas­si­cal chess. {081-C11}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the chess year of 2024
lead.head: Mate in seven lessons

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 81

body: Ajay Shah asked for a tour of chess in 2024. Amit Varma promised more than a tour: in each big chess story of the year, a life les­son that goes be­yond chess and into our lives.

It was a great year for Indian chess, Varma said, though it “ended in a slightly ugly man­ner”. Gukesh Dommaraju won the World Championship, Arjun Erigaisi reached 2809 in the live rat­ings, and India won gold in both sec­tions of the Olympiad.

Shah, old enough to re­mem­ber Anand’s jour­ney, mar­velled that Gukesh was only eigh­teen. Yet he felt no tribal root­ing. Ding, the cham­pion, was to him “an equally won­der­ful flawed char­ac­ter”.
Varma shared the feel­ing. Ding had been world num­ber two in 2019, he said, be­fore Covid and per­sonal trou­bles; win­ning the title then broke him men­tally.
## A change of po­si­tion

The match ended on Ding’s 55. Rf2 in Game 14, a move any half­way de­cent player would avoid in iso­la­tion. But the po­si­tion was not an iso­lated one, Varma ar­gued. Over a few moves the bishop had drifted to a8 and Gukesh’s king had crept two squares closer. Neither player no­ticed the change.

The world is not static, Varma said, and we keep miss­ing that. “Mentally all the time we get stuck with one view of the world, and then ev­ery­thing changes, and we don’t re­alise that it has changed.” {081-C01}

Ding lost the match, in Varma’s read­ing, off the board as much as on it. His team was small and his fit­ness poor, and Gukesh, see­ing that he looked tired, set out to make every game long. “Being good is not enough. It’s the stuff that goes around it that mat­ters,” Varma said. {081-C04}
## Shaped by the road

Gukesh was trained with­out com­put­ers until he be­came a grand­mas­ter. Arjun, short of in­vi­ta­tions to elite events, had to try to win every game in opens. They grew into very dif­fer­ent play­ers.
“It’s not about what you want to do,” Varma said, draw­ing on a scene from Chaitanya Tamhane’s film *The Disciple*. “It’s who do you want to be.” {081-C07}
Magnus Carlsen, he ar­gued, left the clas­si­cal world cham­pi­onship be­cause en­gine prepa­ra­tion had drained the joy out of it. Carlsen chose re­newal over mas­tery, a choice open to all of us.
## Power play
The year’s ugly end be­longed to the same Carlsen: his re­fusal to change out of jeans at the World Rapid in New York, and his pro­posal to split the World Blitz title with Ian Nepomniachtchi.
Power cor­rodes char­ac­ter, Varma warned, and much of suc­cess is luck. The model for han­dling it is Vishy Anand, who has power, “but you would never know”. {081-C12}
Even the cov­er­age car­ried a les­son. Engine bars told view­ers that 55. Rf2 was a blun­der be­fore most could see it for them­selves. Technology, Varma said, should be a tool, not a crutch.
The last word went to Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal, who built ChessBase India for years out of love, with Sagar shoot­ing on his mo­bile phone. It now has mil­lions of sub­scribers.
People over­think new ven­tures, Varma said. “Act today, have a bias for ac­tion, do what you love, things will work out.” {081-C15}

second.label: The Olympiad
second.head: Third board, first prize
second.deck: India’s coach put its top-rated player on board three, and India won gold

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the board-three gambit

body: At the 2024 Olympiad, Arjun Erigaisi was India’s top-rated player. The team coach, Srinath Narayanan, put him on board three, not board one. {081-S06}
His logic, as Amit Varma told it: Arjun is bril­liant at beat­ing play­ers rated 2600, and board three is where he would meet them. If the oth­ers sim­ply drew, India would still win.

Arjun dom­i­nated, and Gukesh, on top board, got some­thing like ten out of eleven. {#tenofeleven} That in­cluded a mirac­u­lous endgame win over Wei Yi, then China’s top-ranked player, which even Hikaru Nakamura praised. Varma called it per­haps the great­est Olympiad per­for­mance of all time, if he was not mis­taken. Both the open and the women’s teams took gold.

quote.text: Why board three? Because he’s bril­liant at beat­ing twenty six hun­dreds, and board three is where he’s likely to play them.

third.head: Look, no computers

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the boy trained without computers

body: When Gukesh was a boy, his coach Vishnu Prasanna went to his par­ents with a pro­posal, as Amit Varma told it: “Let’s do an ex­per­i­ment. Let’s train him with­out com­put­ers.” {081-S04}

Until he be­came a grand­mas­ter, Gukesh ap­par­ently did not use com­put­ers at all. Varma would not say that is the cause, but his cal­cu­la­tion is phe­nom­e­nal: in a com­pli­cated mid­dlegame, “there is no one bet­ter than him”.
Even Magnus Carlsen, Varma said, has found that Gukesh sees lines in post-game talks that never crossed his mind.

The flip side, crit­ics in­clud­ing Carlsen say, is weird po­si­tional in­tu­ition. Varma sus­pects one rea­son. Around 2020 and 2021, four or five Indians would fill the top five at Titled Tuesday, but never Gukesh. {#titletuesday} His rapid and blitz rat­ings sit 100 to 150 points below the top.

p2.title: Lessons from the board
p2.deck: Chess in 2024, chapter by chapter, and the life lesson Amit Varma drew from each, with Ajay Shah’s additions

quote.text: So both these super strong grand­mas­ters were stuck in the old equi­lib­rium. Neither of them re­al­ize what has hap­pened.

box.title: The boy who said he would
box.text: Gukesh, the cham­pion at eigh­teen, was trained with­out com­put­ers until he be­came a grand­mas­ter. At eleven he told Sagar Shah he wanted to be the youngest world cham­pion. “And here we are,” Amit Varma said. {#youngest}

sections.label: The first lesson
sections.head: Stuck in the old equilibrium
sections.caption: Ding’s last blunder
body: Game 14 reached an end­ing in which Gukesh was a pawn up with rooks and bish­ops still on the board. Amit Varma ex­plained that it was a the­o­ret­i­cal draw un­less both rooks and both bish­ops came off.

At move 52 a bishop trade was im­pos­si­ble. By move 54, qui­etly, the white bishop had gone to a8, with only one di­ag­o­nal open, and Gukesh’s king had moved two squares closer. Ding, his mind al­ready on the rapid tiebreak, played 55. Rf2.
Gukesh, who said later that he was about to play Rb3, needed a few sec­onds to see it. Ding re­alised only from Gukesh’s re­ac­tion. Both, Varma said, were stuck in the old equi­lib­rium. {081-S01}
## Strangers in the same house

The les­son, Varma said, is that the world is not static. In work or in love, “the king moves two squares and the bishop goes to A8”, and we do not no­tice. A spe­cial­i­sa­tion gets taken over by AI; a cou­ple ends up as strangers in the same house. {081-C01}

We can­not up­date our pri­ors every minute, Varma con­ceded; it takes too much cog­ni­tive en­ergy. But we set­tle into grooves. Ajay Shah called it sta­tus quo bias, and said wak­ing up to change course is one of life’s great skills. {081-C02}
~ Shah, by his own ac­count a very low qual­ity chess player, was sur­prised to learn that a bishop on a8 can be trapped, with only one di­ag­o­nal to run along.

quote.text: So both these super strong grand­mas­ters were stuck in the old equi­lib­rium. Neither of them re­al­ize what has hap­pened.

sections.label: The second lesson
sections.head: Good is not good enough
sections.caption: the game outside the game
body: The qual­ity of the chess did not de­cide the match, Amit Varma said. Both play­ers made mis­takes; Ding made the last one. What de­cided it was prepa­ra­tion and at­ti­tude, and Ding fell short on both.

His small team meant he was often sur­prised in the open­ing and spent an hour or more re­cov­er­ing. He was also not phys­i­cally fit. As a ju­nior, Varma had learnt that a five-hour game burns as many calo­ries as a boxer loses in a round. {#calories}
Gukesh no­ticed. “Gukesh said he was look­ing tired, so we de­cided I will make him play for as long as pos­si­ble,” Varma re­counted. {081-S02}
## A slight Polish band

Gukesh’s team was built for the job. On Vishy Anand’s sug­ges­tion, Grzegorz Gajewski led it; Jan-Krzysztof Duda played more than 300 prac­tice games with him; Radosław Wojtaszek joined too. “Slight Polish band kind of hap­pen­ing here,” Varma said. {081-J04}

Ajay Shah saw a les­son for Indian firms. It would have been easy to stay clubby, “shar­ing biryani at night” with an all-Indian team. Instead, he said, “They didn’t think in terms of na­tion­al­ity. They just said we’ve got to get a job done.” {081-C05}
~ Shah also saw in­ter­gen­er­a­tional trans­fer at work: Anand brought knowl­edge and cul­ture, and each gen­er­a­tion hands down some­thing bet­ter to the next. {081-C06}

quote.text: Being good is not enough. It’s the stuff that goes around it that mat­ters. It’s the game out­side the game.

sections.label: The third lesson
sections.head: Madman by necessity
sections.caption: Gukesh, Arjun and what shapes us
body: Gukesh and Arjun Erigaisi, Amit Varma said, be­came very dif­fer­ent play­ers be­cause of very dif­fer­ent jour­neys.

Players who cross 2700 usu­ally get in­vited to elite round-robins, where you press with White, ac­cept draws with Black, and six out of ten is a de­cent score. Arjun did not get those in­vi­ta­tions: India al­ready had Pragg, Vidit, Nihal and Harikrishna in the cir­cuit, and no or­gan­iser will call four Indians to a ten-player event.
So he played Swiss-system opens against grand­mas­ters rated 2600 to 2650, where every draw cost him rat­ing points. He had to try to win every game. {081-S05}
He grew so wild that Magnus Carlsen called him a mad­man, and rose from about 2700 to a live peak of 2809, world num­ber two. {#peak-2809}
## What you do, who you be­come

The les­son: what you do shapes who you are. Varma said his own long-form pod­cast­ing, with its de­mands of pa­tience and lis­ten­ing, may even have changed his char­ac­ter. Scrolling and swip­ing puts the mind in one rhythm; read­ing a book or watch­ing good world cin­ema puts it in an­other. {081-C07}
~ Varma com­pared Arjun’s run to Bobby Fischer’s six-nil wins over Taimanov and Larsen, though Fischer’s dom­i­nance, over three play­ers in­clud­ing Petrosian, lasted only a lim­ited pe­riod.

quote.text: In an open tour­na­ment you have to try to win every freak­ing game.

sections.label: The fourth lesson
sections.head: Mugging up is not chess
sections.caption: why Carlsen left the classical crown
body: Magnus Carlsen did not quit the clas­si­cal world cham­pi­onship out of petu­lance, Amit Varma said. He quit be­cause of what en­gines had done to the game.

Engine eval­u­a­tions as­sume per­fect play, and hu­mans never play per­fectly. So elite prepa­ra­tion has be­come a hunt for moves that are not op­ti­mal but whose refu­ta­tion only an­other com­puter could find. {081-C09}

Before each title match, Carlsen and his team spent six months in camp after camp, be­cause an op­po­nent who knew a com­puter line he did not could beat him. {#sixmonths} The qual­ity of his life, he con­cluded in Varma’s telling, had gone to bits. {081-S08}
## Fischer’s old an­swer

His an­swer is freestyle, the new name for Fischer Random or Chess960, which Bobby Fischer de­vised in the 1970s out of the same frus­tra­tion. The pieces be­hind the pawns are shuf­fled iden­ti­cally for both sides, with 960 pos­si­ble start­ing po­si­tions. {#chess-960}

Carlsen has al­ready lost two Chess960 world ti­tles, to Wesley So and Hikaru Nakamura. He plays any­way. “Mastery is good, re­newal is bet­ter,” Varma said: a brain sur­geon who stops read­ing new pa­pers is stuck in his groove. {081-C10}
~ Classical chess is alive, Varma in­sisted: re­ports of its death are ex­ag­ger­ated. But he ex­pects it to die one day, under a moun­tain of the­ory every new­comer must climb.

quote.text: This is not even chess. This is mug­ging up, mug­ging up, mug­ging up. The joy of play­ing chess isn’t there.
quote.who: Magnus Carlsen, as told by Amit Varma

sections.label: The fifth lesson
sections.head: Who will check the king?
sections.caption: Magnus Carlsen’s misbehaviour
body: Magnus Carlsen, Amit Varma said, is eas­ily the great­est player of all time. Fifteen years of dom­i­nance, and a busi­ness through Take Take Take, have given him enor­mous power, and power can af­fect peo­ple in neg­a­tive ways.

In 2022 Carlsen lost to Hans Niemann at the Sinquefield Cup, with­drew and called him a cheat. Varma gave him the ben­e­fit of the doubt at first, then stopped within months. Nobody of­fered a plau­si­ble way to cheat over the board, and Carlsen never apol­o­gised. “Extraordinary claims re­quire ex­tra­or­di­nary ev­i­dence,” Varma said. {081-S09}

Then came Jeansgate, and at the World Blitz a pro­posal to split the title with Ian Nepomniachtchi. Video later caught Carlsen sug­gest­ing that, if FIDE re­fused, they play one short draw after an­other. “It’s ba­si­cally a kind of match fix­ing,” Varma said. {081-S11}
## Judge the act
Borrowing a line from Niemann, Varma asked lis­ten­ers to judge the act, not the name: “for­get it is Magnus Carlsen, for­get it’s the great­est player of all time”. {081-C13}

Power cor­rodes char­ac­ter, he said, and much of suc­cess is luck. Carlsen risks be­com­ing Vladimir Kramnik, a great cham­pion turned em­bit­tered ac­cuser. The model is Vishy Anand: pow­er­ful, soft-spoken, work­ing be­hind the scenes. {081-C12}
~ Varma hoped that Carlsen, who seemed super stressed out through the last day of blitz, comes out of this phase.

quote.text: Do you think Vishy Anand doesn’t have power? Oh man, he has power. But you would never know.

portraits.caption: Magnus Carlsen
portraits.credit: Andreas Kontokanis from Piraeus, Greece, CC BY-SA 2.0

sections.label: The sixth lesson
sections.head: Engine on, brain off
sections.caption: computers and coverage
body: Amit Varma watched 55. Rf2 on Sagar Shah’s stream. The mo­ment it was played, the com­puter eval­u­a­tion changed on screen and ev­ery­body stood up. Only Tania Sachdev, he thought, worked it out from the board; even Sagar glanced at the com­puter to make sure.
On David Howell’s broad­cast there was no en­gine eval­u­a­tion. Howell took about as long as Gukesh to see the blun­der, Varma said, be­cause he was think­ing on his own. {081-S14}
## A tool, not a crutch

The les­son reaches be­yond chess. Use ChatGPT for ideas and to pol­ish your prose, Varma said, but do the writ­ing your­self so your brain keeps work­ing. “If you use it as a crutch, you dumb your­self down.” {081-C14}
Ajay Shah’s gloss was shorter: “you stop ex­pe­ri­enc­ing life”. Varma agreed, be­cause you stop think­ing about the chess.
Varma also bris­tled at au­di­ences who clap when a player finds the engine’s top move. “Are you guys mo­rons? There are prob­a­bly four or five moves which are fine here.” {081-J07}
~ His ad­vice to view­ers: watch cov­er­age in which strong grand­mas­ters talk about the po­si­tion, with the eval­u­a­tion bar switched off.

quote.text: Howell took as much time to fig­ure out it’s a blun­der as Gukesh did. You can ac­tu­ally time them.
And Sagar and Amruta showed us a way by div­ing into some­thing for the love of it. And that’s my les­son to ev­ery­one. If you’re watch­ing this, that’s all you need.

p3.title: Stories of the year
p3.deck: Jeans, a guru’s silence, a president’s reply and a channel built on love

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Magnus Carlsen, a dress code and FIDE
stories.head: A principle nobody could name
body: The World Rapid Championship in New York, held on Wall Street and planned by FIDE for months, was mag­nif­i­cently or­gan­ised, Amit Varma said. Magnus Carlsen started badly, with two and a half points out of five on day one. {#twoandhalf}

On day two he showed up in jeans, oth­er­wise per­fectly turned out in blazer and boots. Every player signs up to the dress code, and jeans break it. Ian Nepomniachtchi, that day or the day be­fore, had been told to change out of sneak­ers, and did.

The players’ rooms were three min­utes away. Carlsen was told he need not change at once, only be­fore round nine. He re­fused, and later said on Take Take Take that he had de­cided on prin­ci­ple not to change. {081-S10}

Varma won­dered “what is this prin­ci­ple that on prin­ci­ple you refuse to fol­low a rule”. FIDE, bound to treat ev­ery­one equally, would not pair him. Carlsen with­drew from the Rapid and the Blitz, and on Take Take Take said “Fuck you” to FIDE “in ex­actly these many words”. {081-J08}

Varma thinks the rule it­self stupid; Jimmy Carter, he noted, made jeans ac­cept­able as pres­i­dent. But the rule was there and ev­ery­one had agreed to it. Had Carlsen been win­ning, Varma doubted there would have been a tantrum.

Then Carlsen went over the heads of the chief ex­ec­u­tive, Emil Sutovsky, and the vice-president, Vishy Anand, to the pres­i­dent, Arkady Dvorkovich, who let him back into the Blitz in jeans. There were, Carlsen said, “no grown-ups in FIDE”, and Anand was not up for the job.
~ Varma called it out­ra­geous be­hav­iour. Sutovsky and Anand, he said, are com­plete gen­tle­men.
stories.why: FIDE’s hands were tied, Amit Varma ar­gued: it has to treat ev­ery­one equally. But a bad mood met star power, and a plain dress code be­came an ego thing, set­tled only when the pres­i­dent gave way.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s film recommendation, and a guru’s condition
stories.head: Join the band, leave the class
body: In Chaitanya Tamhane’s film *The Disciple*, Sharad Nerulkar is a purist singer of Hindustani clas­si­cal music who teaches a class. One day a student’s mother waits pa­tiently to speak to him.

Her son wants to join a col­lege fu­sion band, she says. One mem­ber will sing Western rock in English; her son will sing the clas­si­cal music he has been taught. He will not join with­out his guru’s per­mis­sion, and his mother clearly wants him to.
Nerulkar tells the boy that yes, he can join them. A mo­ment of si­lence fol­lows. Then he adds: “But don’t come for class any­more.” {081-S07}
~ Bizarre as it may seem, Amit Varma said, the point is that what you do shapes what you are. The boy was nowhere near ready, and the choice was his: who did he want to be? {081-C07}
stories.why: Doing some­thing again and again changes the kind of per­son you be­come. Amit Varma’s test for the scroll or the book is the same as the guru’s: not what you want to do, but who you want to be.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on a guru, a band and a choice

stories.kicker: Two stories from Salil Tripathi, retold by Amit Varma
stories.head: First, let the hungry speak
body: The jour­nal­ist Salil Tripathi, Amit Varma’s guest on a com­ing episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, once put a ques­tion to Václav Havel, then head of state of Czechoslovakia, at a press con­fer­ence.

Some argue, Salil said, that free speech is not the most im­por­tant right, and that you have to feed peo­ple first. Havel dis­agreed: “Because with­out free speech, how will a hun­gry man even be able to com­mu­ni­cate that he’s hun­gry?” {081-S12}

Then Havel asked who ar­gued oth­er­wise. The per­son you are meet­ing this af­ter­noon, Salil replied: Lee Kuan Yew. Silence fell over the hall. Then Havel said that in that case, he would make sure he told him he was wrong.
~ Varma loved the anec­dote for what it tells you about what a prin­ci­pled man Havel was.
stories.why: Havel held his line when it was diplo­mat­i­cally awk­ward. Power cor­rupts, as the say­ing goes, and ab­so­lute power cor­rupts ab­so­lutely; not only in gov­ern­ments, Varma said: power and suc­cess can cor­rode anyone’s char­ac­ter. {081-J17}
stories.postscript: Nelson Mandela, asked by Salil to speak up for Aung San Suu Kyi, de­clined: “that was pris­oner Mandela. This is President Mandela.” {081-S13}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Havel and Lee Kuan Yew

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the couple behind ChessBase India
stories.head: A mobile phone and a long game
body: The morn­ing after Gukesh won, Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal flew to Singapore. Gukesh hugged Sagar, then saw Amruta, and went and hugged her too. These two, Amit Varma said, are so im­por­tant to Indian chess.

Sagar, an International Master who never made grand­mas­ter, ran ChessBase India with Amruta for years as a labour of love. “Often he would just go and he would shoot with his mo­bile phone, using the sound of the mo­bile phone,” Varma said. {081-S15}

He went to under-11 and dis­trict events and talked to small kids and women play­ers. For three, four, five years, Varma thinks, the views went nowhere. {#views} During Covid, with help from the co­me­dian Samay Raina, the chan­nel ex­ploded; it now has mil­lions of sub­scribers.
~ One old clip shows an eleven-year-old Gukesh telling Sagar he wants to be the youngest world cham­pion.
stories.why: Varma would give the sec­ond Bharat Ratna for chess, after Vishy Anand, to these two. People over­think new ven­tures, he said; Sagar and Amruta sim­ply kept show­ing up, for years, out of love. {081-C15}

quiz.q: Which move in Game 14 handed Gukesh the world title?
quiz.a: 55. Rf2, al­low­ing a rook trade and then a forced bishop trade.

quiz.q: Why did Srinath Narayanan put India’s top-rated player, Arjun Erigaisi, on board three at the Olympiad?
quiz.a: Arjun is bril­liant at beat­ing 2600-rated play­ers, and board three is where he’d face them.

quiz.q: What experiment did Vishnu Prasanna propose to the young Gukesh’s parents?
quiz.a: To train him with­out com­put­ers, which he ap­par­ently did until he be­came a grand­mas­ter.

quiz.q: According to a factoid Amit Varma learnt as a junior, what does a five-hour game burn?
quiz.a: As many calo­ries as a boxer loses in a round of box­ing.

quiz.q: Why did Ajay Shah think Gukesh’s team held a lesson for Indian firms?
quiz.a: It was built for the job, not na­tion­al­ity: al­most en­tirely a multi­na­tional team.

quiz.q: What did Nelson Mandela tell Salil Tripathi when asked to speak up for Aung San Suu Kyi?
quiz.a: That was pris­oner Mandela; this was President Mandela, im­pris­oned by the pres­i­dency.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 81. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Magnus Carlsen (Andreas Kontokanis from Piraeus, Greece, CC BY-SA 2.0); Gukesh D (Frans Peeters, CC BY-SA 2.0); Ding Liren (Stefan64, CC BY-SA 3.0); Viswanathan Anand (Wolfgang Jekel, CC BY 2.0); Arjun Erigaisi (Frans Peeters, CC BY-SA 2.0); Bobby Fischer (Bert Verhoeff for Anefo, CC0); Vladimir Kramnik (Vladimir Barskij, CC BY-SA 3.0); Chaitanya Tamhane (Bollywood Hungama, CC BY 3.0); Hikaru Nakamura (Andreas Kontokanis from Piraeus, Greece - photo DS28 - crop., CC BY-SA 2.0); Emil Sutovsky (Stefan64, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: The Disciple
shelf.creator: Chaitanya Tamhane
shelf.why: Its scene where a purist guru tells a stu­dent he can join a fu­sion band but must stop com­ing to class cap­tures the idea that what you do de­ter­mines who you be­come.

shelf.title: Traffic
shelf.creator: Tom Vanderbilt
shelf.why: Vanderbilt doc­u­ments that a large share of ac­ci­dents hap­pen close to home, when fa­mil­iar ground makes driv­ers switch off, which is ex­actly what hap­pened to Ajay on a hike.

shelf.title: A Meditation on Form
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s essay on how form dic­tates con­tent: long-form pod­cast­ing is a dif­fer­ent ac­tiv­ity from short-form, not a longer ver­sion of it, and its pa­tience, lis­ten­ing and cu­rios­ity changed him as a host and per­haps as a per­son.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Chess (Episode 52)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A syn­the­sis of Amit’s knowl­edge of and en­thu­si­asm for chess, walk­ing through every world cham­pion up to Ding and the role of com­put­ers in the game.

shelf.title: The Hiking Episode (Episode 35)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay on his pas­sion for hik­ing, from the Goecha La trek be­neath Kanchenjunga to why the worst ac­ci­dents hap­pen when you think you’re al­most home.

shelf.title: Chess.com report on Gukesh’s win, with analysis of Game 14 by Rafael Leitao
shelf.creator: Rafael Leitao
shelf.why: Lets you see for your­self how the po­si­tion drifted (bishop to a8, king two squares closer) be­fore 55.

shelf.title: Gukesh interviewed at length by Sagar Shah after the World Championship
shelf.creator: Sagar Shah
shelf.why: Source for Gukesh say­ing he was about to play Rb3, and for his plan to make every game long be­cause Ding looked tired.

shelf.title: Jan-Krzysztof Duda interviewed by Sagar Shah
shelf.creator: Sagar Shah
shelf.why: Duda, who played 300+ prac­tice games with Gukesh, says his help might have mat­tered more in a tiebreak than in the clas­si­cal games.

shelf.title: Vishnu Prasanna interviewed by Sagar Shah
shelf.creator: Sagar Shah
shelf.why: Gukesh’s early coach ex­plains his ex­per­i­ment of train­ing Gukesh with­out com­put­ers until he be­came a GM.

shelf.title: Hikaru Nakamura on Gukesh’s game against Wei Yi
shelf.creator: Hikaru Nakamura
shelf.why: Even com­men­ta­tors who rarely give credit called the endgame mirac­u­lous.

shelf.title: Live Chess Ratings (2700chess.com)
shelf.why: Tracks the top players’ live rat­ings, where Arjun reached world num­ber two.

shelf.title: Magnus Carlsen’s interview on Take Take Take about Freestyle Chess
shelf.creator: Take Take Take
shelf.why: Carlsen ex­plains why he sees freestyle (Chess960) as the most alive form of chess now.

shelf.title: Hans Niemann interviewed in 2022 about his alleged cheating
shelf.why: Niemann ad­mits his past on­line cheat­ing as a teenager and in­sists it is be­hind him, which is his side of the story.

shelf.title: Magnus Carlsen on Jeansgate
shelf.creator: Take Take Take
shelf.why: Carlsen says he re­fused to change ‘on principle’ and lashes out at FIDE.

shelf.title: Magnus Carlsen on getting his way
shelf.creator: Take Take Take
shelf.why: Here he says there are ‘no grown-ups in FIDE’ and that Anand is not up for his job, the be­hav­iour Amit calls de­plorable.

shelf.title: Emil Sutovsky about the organisation of the event
shelf.creator: Emil Sutovsky
shelf.why: The FIDE CEO’s own view; Amit praises his con­duct through­out as gen­tle­manly.

shelf.title: The match fixing suggestion (X post)
shelf.why: The viral footage be­hind Amit’s charge that it amounted to a kind of match fix­ing.

shelf.title: Upcoming episode of The Seen and the Unseen with Salil Tripathi
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Salil Tripathi tells the Havel and Mandela sto­ries that Amit uses to show how power changes peo­ple, in­clud­ing Havel’s moral clar­ity in power.

shelf.title: ChessBase India
shelf.creator: Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal
shelf.why: Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal’s chess plat­form, which began as a labour of love (cov­er­ing ob­scure tour­na­ments, in­ter­view­ing play­ers, analysing games) and pi­o­neered using com­put­ers to il­lu­mi­nate the game.

shelf.title: Sagar & Amruta meeting Gukesh in Singapore
shelf.creator: Sagar Shah
shelf.why: Gukesh hugs Sagar and then Amruta, show­ing how much the two mean to Indian chess.

shelf.title: Gukesh stating his ambition to Sagar Shah at age 11
shelf.creator: Sagar Shah
shelf.why: An 11-year-old Gukesh says he wants to be the youngest world cham­pion, and now he is.

shelf.title: Sagar Shah at the under-11 workshop all those years ago
shelf.creator: Sagar Shah
shelf.why: Sagar ex­plains po­si­tions to kids on the floor, in­clud­ing Gukesh, Pranav and Leon Luke Mendonca, with Gukesh’s dad in the back­ground.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A ten-and-a-half-hour con­ver­sa­tion with Ajay about his life and ideas, in­clud­ing the in­side story of how India built a good eq­uity mar­ket through SEBI, NSE and NSDL.

laughs.text: A wink at their own course name: Amit on call­ing ev­ery­thing ‘life lessons’: ‘Well I mean, why not? We haven’t trade­marked it be­cause like who cares?’
Ajay in­tro­duc­ing a fa­mil­iar maxim with a straight face: ‘The great philoso­pher Bill Gates says...’
Amit’s Hindi riff on over­es­ti­mat­ing the short term, the ‘sab badal jayega... viral ho jayega’ (ev­ery­thing will change, it’ll go viral) fan­tasy, fol­lowed by: ‘noth­ing hap­pens.’
On Gukesh’s sec­onds Gajewski, Duda and Wojtaszek: ‘Slight Polish band kind of hap­pen­ing here.’
Ajay on the cosier al­ter­na­tive of an all-Indian team: ‘the com­fort of the re­la­tion­ships and shar­ing biryani at night.’
Amit on au­di­ences clap­ping when Gukesh found the engine’s top move: ‘Are you guys mo­rons? There are prob­a­bly four or five moves which are fine here.’
Carlsen, per Amit, went on Take Take Take and said ‘Fuck you’ to FIDE ‘in ex­actly these many words’, and later com­plained there are ‘no grown-ups in FIDE.’
Jeansgate: Carlsen’s re­fusal to change out of jeans at the New York World Rapid. Amit notes Jimmy Carter fa­mously made jeans ac­cept­able as pres­i­dent, adding RIP since he had passed re­cently.
The ‘vi­brat­ing anal beads’ the­ory of how Niemann might have cheated, retweeted by Elon Musk. Amit: ‘shit like that was never se­ri­ous.’
Chess as a phys­i­cal sport: from Amit’s ju­nior days, the fac­toid that a five-hour clas­si­cal game burns as many calo­ries as a boxer uses in a round. Anand fa­mously did yoga to stay fit.
Peter Leko, Keymer’s coach, once led Kramnik 6-5 in a World Championship match. Kramnik won the last game to tie, and as the in­cum­bent kept the title, ‘bit of a tragedy.’
Bobby Fischer’s 6-0 sweeps of Taimanov and Larsen, and his win over Petrosian, as the clos­est par­al­lel to Arjun’s dom­i­nance of 2600-level grand­mas­ters.

Chess960 (Fischer Random): Bobby Fischer’s 1970s an­swer to open­ing drudgery, with back-rank pieces shuf­fled iden­ti­cally for both sides across 960 pos­si­ble starts. Carlsen re­brands it as ‘freestyle.’ Amit on clas­si­cal chess: re­ports of its death are ex­ag­ger­ated.
Amit’s hy­po­thet­i­cal Bharat Ratna for chess: the first to Vishy Anand, the sec­ond jointly to Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal.
